identity.title: Unlocking the Capabilities of Thought: A Reasoning Boundary Framework to Quantify and Optimize Chain-of-Thought

problem.claim: The paper addresses how to quantify and optimize chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning capabilities in large language models on complex reasoning tasks.

gap.claim: Existing research lacks quantitative metrics for CoT capabilities and guidance for improving CoT performance.

contributions.claim: Introduces a reasoning boundary framework (RBF) for quantifying and optimizing CoT.
Defines a reasoning boundary as a CoT upper bound, establishes a combination law, and proposes three RB categories with laws for RB promotion and reasoning-path optimization.
Makes the code and data publicly available.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe RBF as a novel framework intended to address the identified quantification and optimization challenges.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments across 27 models and 5 tasks that validate the existence and rationality of the proposed framework.
The authors report that the framework explains the effectiveness of 10 CoT strategies and guides optimization from two perspectives.

narrative_sequence.summary: CoT is presented as a promising approach for improving LLM performance on complex reasoning tasks, while prior work studies its mechanisms.
The paper identifies missing quantitative capability metrics and insufficient optimization guidance.
RBF is introduced, with reasoning boundaries and a combination law for quantification, plus three RB categories for optimization.
The categories are further developed through RB-promotion and reasoning-path optimization laws.
The authors report multi-model, multi-task experiments, explanations of 10 CoT strategies, and optimization guidance.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns separate gaps with separate framework components: reasoning boundaries and combination laws target quantification, while RB categories and optimization laws target improvement.

lessons.interpretation: Explicitly mapping each claimed limitation to a method component can make a technical contribution easier to evaluate conceptually.
lessons.application: When framing a new method, pair each stated gap with a named mechanism and indicate how the mechanism addresses it.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the task has one inseparable bottleneck or when the proposed components do not correspond to independently stated needs.

unknowns: The abstract does not define the reasoning-boundary formalism or the three RB categories.
Experimental datasets, baselines, metrics, and the meanings of “existence,” “rationality,” and “two perspectives” are unspecified.
The abstract does not provide quantitative results for the 27 models, 5 tasks, or 10 strategies.
